summary:
Omer Primor, leading product marketing at Bright Data, argues the web should be treated as decaying context for agentic AI rather than static data: social content is stale within a day and news, finance, and retail data is largely irrelevant after 30 days, making context extraction an ongoing process. He traces search evolution from Google's two-decade dominance to in-LLM web search (1.5–2 years ago) and the rise of AI-native engines like Exa, Parallel, you.com, and Tavily, with Amazon and Microsoft also launching agent-oriented retrieval. He introduces Context-as-a-Service (CaaS) as vertical, knowledge-graph-backed providers exposing domain-specific data via MCP, CLI, or API across e-commerce, travel, finance, market research, HR, and real estate, noting incumbents like ZoomInfo repositioning with agent-targeted brands such as gtm.ai.

In a 25-field enrichment test run 100 times against the event's sponsors using an Opus 4.8-driven agent loop, coverage showed strong convergence among AI search and one major CaaS provider, while two CaaS providers placed lower, an outcome Primor explained as a coverage ceiling: CaaS can only answer from data it already holds. Cost results showed AI search, CaaS, and Google-based retrieval converging to similar per-record cost (the CaaS fee on top of token burn from the agent loop), with one outlier CaaS that he declined to name being far more expensive and another niche CaaS positioned as cheap low-quality longtail.

Primor's core claim is that every repeated query costs the same as the first, so teams quietly cut corners: refreshing weekly instead of daily, taking 10 results instead of all, or skipping questions. He framed this as renting versus owning context. To illustrate the alternative, Bright Data built a one-day DIY pipeline using two dedicated scrapers (LinkedIn Companies and LinkedIn Jobs via Crunchbase, plus a new AI-powered Scraper Studio with self-healing), merged into one entity with simple heuristics, producing zero-token coverage that stacked up reasonably well. Pricing setup at one week and $5,000, the DIY path crossed over with renting at just above 15,000 entities or queries; he stresses the real crossover likely sits lower than most teams assume. Above that tipping point, upfront investment makes subsequent retrieval effectively free, eliminating corner-cutting, enabling custom business logic, and compounding over time. He concludes that owned context compounds while rented context keeps decaying, and recommends mixing AI search and CaaS for ad hoc needs while building owned pipelines for persistent, escalating knowledge work.

sections.title: Web scale, and the web as context rather than data
sections.summary: Primor introduces himself and Bright Data's scale (over 50 billion HTML pages per day, 20+ petabytes of media, 20,000 teams, 70%+ of top AI labs), then argues the web should be treated as context for AI agents rather than static data, because AI knowledge work needs continuously refreshed information.

sections.title: Data decay, and why context is not a snapshot
sections.summary: Using an internal decay chart, he shows social content is stale within a day and news, finance, and retail are largely irrelevant after 30 days, concluding that web context extraction is an ongoing process, not a one-time snapshot.

sections.title: Search fragments, from Google to the AI search companies
sections.summary: He traces a three-stage search evolution: Google's 20-year dominance, in-LLM web search emerging 1.5–2 years ago, and the rise of AI-native search companies (Exa, Parallel, you.com, Tavily), with Amazon and Microsoft also launching agent-oriented web retrieval products.

sections.title: What search cannot answer about change over time
sections.summary: He argues search only tells part of the story: queries like 'price of sneakers this morning' can be answered, but longitudinal questions (price changes, hiring trends over time) cannot, even when the underlying data exists.

sections.title: Context as a service, and the vertical search shape
sections.summary: He introduces CaaS as vertical, knowledge-graph-backed providers exposing domain-specific data via MCP, CLI, or API across e-commerce, travel, finance, market research, HR, and real estate, and notes incumbents like ZoomInfo repositioning with agent-targeted brands such as gtm.ai. He frames this as web context engineering.

sections.title: The test: 25 fields, 100 companies
sections.summary: He describes a non-benchmark test: enrich one entity across 25 fields using an Opus 4.8-driven agent loop with budget guardrails, run 100 times against the event's sponsors. Coverage results show strong convergence among AI search and one major CaaS provider, while two CaaS providers placed lower, an outcome he explains as a coverage ceiling: CaaS can only answer from data it already holds.

sections.title: Coverage ceiling of CaaS and cost convergence across vendors
sections.summary: He explains why the two lower-placing CaaS providers cannot answer questions outside what they have already collected, unlike search, and notes coverage depends on the specific job at hand. He then turns to cost, showing AI search, CaaS, and Google-based retrieval converge to similar per-record cost once token burn from the agent loop is included, with one unnamed CaaS provider far more expensive and one cheaper secondary CaaS positioned as lower-quality longtail.

sections.title: Frequency as the cost killer and the rise of corner-cutting
sections.summary: He reframes the cost question as a million-record problem in frequency rather than volume: every repeated query costs the same as the first even when the answer is identical, and high token burn does not shrink over time. Teams respond by renting context and cutting corners: refreshing weekly instead of daily, accepting 10 results instead of all, or skipping questions entirely, forgoing value to control cost.

sections.title: Building it yourself in a day
sections.summary: As an alternative, his engineer built a DIY pipeline in about a day: two dedicated scrapers for LinkedIn Companies, LinkedIn Jobs, and Crunchbase via pay-as-you-go, plus Bright Data's new Scraper Studio (an AI tool that builds a scraper for any website in under 5 minutes with self-healing), merged into one entity with simple conflict-resolution heuristics. The result was reasonable coverage with zero AI token cost, though not as good as the best test runs, and Primor stresses it is a test, not a production benchmark.

sections.title: The tipping point just above 15,000 queries
sections.summary: Pricing the DIY setup at one week and $5,000, he plots a build-vs-rent crossover showing the DIY path crosses the renting path at just above 15,000 entities or queries, and argues the real crossover for many teams is probably lower than they assume. Above the tipping point, upfront investment makes later retrieval effectively free, eliminating corner-cutting and enabling custom business logic.

sections.title: Owned context compounds, rented context decays
sections.summary: He closes by recommending AI search and CaaS for ad hoc, always-changing needs, possibly mixed and matched with lighter models, but warns frequency eventually becomes the cost killer. The core takeaway is that owned context compounds while rented context keeps decaying, and a million-query horizon is what matters, not the 15,000-query tipping point.

demonstrations: A non-benchmark test enriching one entity across 25 fields using an Opus 4.8-driven agent loop with budget guardrails, executed 100 times against event sponsors.
A side-by-side coverage and cost comparison across AI search, major and secondary CaaS providers, Google-based retrieval, and Cloud's native search.

A one-day DIY enrichment pipeline using two dedicated scrapers (LinkedIn Companies, LinkedIn Jobs, Crunchbase) plus Scraper Studio with self-healing, merged into one entity via simple conflict-resolution heuristics, yielding zero-token cost and reasonable coverage.
A build-vs-rent crossover visualization plotting per-record cost against volume, showing the DIY path crossing the renting path just above 15,000 entities when setup is priced at $5,000.
limitations: CaaS providers can only answer from what they already hold, so out-of-corpus questions have no answer at any price, and coverage comparisons depend heavily on the specific job.
The speaker explicitly frames both the 25-field test and the DIY scraper build as tests, not benchmarks, with no claim to broad statistical confidence.
The enrichment test was run only against the event's sponsors, a small and non-representative entity set.
The DIY pipeline used simple conflict-resolution heuristics and was built in about a day, so it is not directly comparable to production-grade, out-of-the-box APIs.
The crossover figure of ~15,000 entities depends on pricing setup at exactly $5,000 and one week of work, and could realistically be anywhere from 10,000 to 100,000 depending on use case.

organization.name: Bright Data
organization.summary: Bright Data is an independent web-data company (formerly Luminati Networks) that sells public-web collection infrastructure for humans and AI agents. First-party pages describe a platform of ethically sourced proxy networks, Web Access APIs, dynamically refreshed datasets, and AI-ready interfaces including an MCP server. The homepage and docs present Scraper Studio as the IDE and AI agent for building, previewing, and self-healing custom scrapers that can be triggered by API or schedule. Omer Primor leads product marketing there and used Scraper Studio in the talk's owned-context demo. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and named search vendors are mentioned comparables, not the implementation owner.
organization.status: Independent company as of the research date. Homepage, about page, and docs.brightdata.com are live. About page states 20,000+ organizations; homepage markets 50,000+ customers. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.
